subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Enhanced Fujita Scale
description: A 60-second lesson on The Enhanced Fujita Scale.

hook.text: An EF0 tornado snaps tree branches. An EF5 rips houses off their foundations entirely.

buildup.text: The Enhanced Fujita Scale rates tornadoes from EF0 to EF5 based on damage, not wind speed.

discovery.text: Tornado winds can't be measured directly. Scientists assess damage to estimate peak speeds.

twist.text: EF5 tornadoes are extremely rare — fewer than one per year on average in the US.

climax.text: The 2011 Joplin, Missouri EF5 tornado killed 158 people in less than 30 minutes.

punchline.text: We rate tornadoes by what they leave behind — or don't.

quiz.question: How is a tornado's EF rating determined?
options: By assessing the damage it causes

details.summary: The Enhanced Fujita scale rates tornado intensity from EF0 to EF5 based on observed damage to specific structures rather than direct wind measurement. An EF5 tornado produces estimated winds over 322 km/h and can sweep away well-built homes from their foundations.
details.whyItMatters: The EF scale standardizes tornado reporting and helps engineers design buildings that can withstand tornado winds. It also reveals how few tornadoes are truly catastrophic.
takeaways: EF5 tornadoes have estimated winds over 322 km/h
Over 90 percent of tornadoes are EF2 or weaker
The scale uses 28 damage indicators including different building types

faq.question: Why not measure tornado winds directly?
faq.answer: Tornadoes are small and unpredictable, making it nearly impossible to place instruments in the path of the strongest winds. Most anemometers are destroyed or never hit. The EF scale uses structural damage analysis as a proxy for peak wind speeds.

faq.question: How common are EF5 tornadoes?
faq.answer: Only about 0.1 percent of all tornadoes reach EF5 intensity. The US averages roughly one EF5 tornado per year, but a single one can devastate entire communities, as seen in Joplin, Missouri in 2011.
